papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation.
papers.abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

papers.title: Circadian and Sleep-Wake Modulation of EEG Functional Connectivity Across Brain States and Its Associations With Cognition in Humans.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythms both influence human brain function, but their distinct contributions to large-scale network organization remain unclear. We quantified the effect of brain state (wake, NREM, REM), sleep-wake history, and circadian phase on functional connectivity using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG recorded during a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol. We derived principal components of functional connectivity and found that both sleep-wake history and circadian phase significantly modulated functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history exerting a broader influence. Complementary cosinor analyses further demonstrated circadian rhythmicity in several NREM and REM connectivity measures. Across sleep, global connectivity increased progressively during NREM sleep, particularly in the delta and sigma bands, but declined during REM sleep. During controlled resting wakefulness, increasing time awake was associated with higher global alpha-band connectivity, which was associated with poorer concurrent cognitive performance. Connectivity during NREM sleep was also associated with subsequent cognitive performance, with lower global theta and, to a lesser extent, higher sigma connectivity linked to better performance. REM connectivity was not associated with these cognitive measures. Together, these findings reveal opposing NREM and REM trajectories in large-scale EEG functional connectivity and show that these brain-state-specific network dynamics are shaped by both sleep-wake history and circadian phase and are associated with cognitive performance.

papers.title: Layer 1 NDNF interneurons form distinct subpopulations with opposite activation patterns during sleep in freely behaving mice
papers.abstract: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep facilitates memory consolidation by transferring information from the hippocampus to the neocortex. This transfer is thought to occur primarily when hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) and thalamocortical spindles are synchronized. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the role of cortical layer 1 NDNF-expressing (L1 NDNF) interneurons in gating information transfer during SWR-spindle synchronization in NREM sleep. Using simultaneous cell-specific calcium imaging with a head-mounted microscope and local field potential recordings in freely moving mice, we compared the activity of L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons across vigilance states and during NREM-specific oscillations. Our findings reveal that L1 NDNF neurons form three distinct populations, assembling into cell networks tuned to specific sleep stages. REM active L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons exhibit opposite activation patterns during spindles. While L2/3 cells are mostly inactive during SWR, NREM, and REM active L1 NDNF cells inhibit the network upon SWR onset depending on their coupling with spindles. L1 NDNF neurons mediate slow inhibition primarily via GABAB receptors. Systemic application of a GABAB receptor antagonist resulted in decreased neuronal coupling of pyramidal cells but did not change the inhibitory responses during SWRs. Overall, these findings highlight the potential role of L1 NDNF neuron-mediated inhibition in the response to synchronized sleep oscillations, with potential implications for memory consolidation.

papers.title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.

papers.title: Behavioral, Transcriptomic, and Neuroinflammatory Effects of Sleep Deprivation: Insights From Separate Acute and Chronic Experimental Paradigms.
papers.abstract: Depression is a global health burden associated with sleep disruption and inflammation. While acute sleep deprivation (ASD) can alleviate depressive symptoms, chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) is a risk factor for mood disorders. However, the contrasting mechanisms underlying these opposing outcomes remain poorly understood. We integrated behavioral profiling, multi-region transcriptomics, and multiplex cytokine analysis to separately characterize the effects of ASD in a pain-depression comorbidity model and CSD in normal mice. Adult male C57BL/6J mice (n = 6 per group) were subjected to either a single 6-h total sleep deprivation (ASD) or 6-h daily sleep deprivation for 14 consecutive days (CSD). Behavioral testing included the tail suspension test (TST), open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), and sucrose preference test (SPT). Following the interventions, five brain regions-prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), agranular insular cortex (AI), parietal cortex (PAR), and retrosplenial cortex (RSP)-were dissected. Cytokine levels were quantified using a multiplex panel targeting 15 analytes. Behavioral tests demonstrated that ASD alleviated despair-like behaviors induced by spared nerve injury surgery, whereas CSD resulted in anxiety- and despair-like behaviors. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) exhibited prominent transcriptomic responses to both ASD and CSD, with a substantial number of differentially expressed mRNAs. Transcriptome sequencing confirmed stable differential expression of mRNAs across multiple brain regions. Notable genes linked to depression, including Plin4 and Sult1a1, emerged as potential targets for further research. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of differentially expressed mRNAs in the PFC indicated that IL-6 and TNF were primarily associated with these changes following ASD. Additionally, inflammatory factors such as BAFF, CHI3L1, IL-4, IL-6R alpha, IL-6, IL-10, TNFRSF1B, IL-12 p70, TWEAK, and osteopontin significantly decreased in the ASD group but increased in the CSD group. This study elucidates that ASD is associated with alleviation of despair-like behaviors and concurrent suppression of multiple inflammatory factors; however, the causal relationship between these observations requires further experimental validation. These findings open new research avenues for identifying potential depression treatment targets. Future research should explore the functional implications of these transcriptomic changes and their relevance for developing novel antidepressant strategies. These findings open new research avenues for identifying potential depression treatment targets. papers.title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
papers.abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce \textbf{SleepPairNet}, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.

papers.title: Phasic pupil responses to melanopsin- and cone-directed stimulation remain stable across circadian time
papers.abstract: Human pupil responses vary with time of day, but whether this reflects circadian modulation of specific photoreceptor pathways is unclear. Twelve healthy adults completed repeated pupillometry during a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake protocol that limited sustained wakefulness; data from eight met the quality-control criteria and were analysed. This design was intended to limit progressive accumulation of homeostatic sleep pressure across sampled circadian phase. During wake episodes, 0.4-Hz silent-substitution stimuli targeted broadband flux, melanopsin, luminance, L-M cone-opponent, or S-cone pathways. Salivary melatonin provided participant-specific period estimates. We separated slow tonic constriction from phasic pupil tracking and compared hierarchical circadian cosinor models with constant-level models. Constant-level models were favoured for phasic amplitude in all five conditions (log10 BF10 = -3.36 to -1.10). They were also favoured for tonic minimum in four conditions; L-M favoured the circadian model (log10 BF10 = 0.67), but the evidence was imprecise. Under the tested contrast, adaptation, and frequency, these data do not support circadian modulation of phasic photoreceptor-directed pupil tracking. Other metrics and smaller or non-sinusoidal effects remain possible.

papers.title: Sleep stage-specific heart rate variability feature-driven clustering analysis: identifying cardiac autonomic endotypes with long-term cardiovascular predictive value.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular risk assessment in obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) has traditionally relied on the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). However, AHI primarily reflects respiratory event burden and may not adequately capture inter-individual heterogeneity in sleep-related cardiorespiratory regulation. This study aimed to identify sleep stage-specific heart rate variability (HRV) phenotypes and evaluate their associations with long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Data were obtained from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS). After exclusion of participants with missing clinical covariates or outcome data, 4029 individuals were included. Linear and non-linear HRV features were extracted from stage-specific electrocardiographic segments during N2, N3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. K-means clustering was performed independently for each sleep stage after Z-score standardization, and the optimal cluster number was determined using silhouette coefficients and the elbow method. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier analyses were used to evaluate associations between HRV-informed phenotypes and all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Three HRV-informed phenotypes were identified within the selected clustering framework across N2, N3, and REM sleep stages: Stable (Cluster 0), Burden (Cluster 1), and High risk (Cluster 2). Compared with the Stable phenotype, the High-risk phenotype was consistently associated with increased cardiovascular risk, with the strongest association observed for incident CVD in the N2 stage [hazard ratio (HR) 1.468, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.280-1.684, P < 0.001]. Similar associations were observed in the N3 (HR 1.426, 95% CI 1.249-1.629, P < 0.001) and REM (HR 1.394, 95% CI 1.216-1.598, P < 0.001) stages. Sequential adjustment for AHI, oxygen desaturation index, arousal index, and sleep efficiency resulted in only minimal attenuation of hazard estimates, indicating that the prognostic associations were largely independent of conventional respiratory severity measures. In contrast, the Burden phenotype was consistently associated with lower all-cause mortality across all three sleep stages (HR 0.83-0.85, all P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses stratified by OSA severity demonstrated broadly consistent prognostic associations across AHI strata. Incorporating sleep stage-specific HRV features into conventional clinical phenotyping provides complementary prognostic information beyond traditional respiratory severity metrics. HRV-informed phenotyping may improve long-term cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with OSA.

papers.title: Sleep Stage Classification Across Heterogeneous EEG/EOG Channels with Multi-channel Differential Transformer.
papers.abstract: Classification of sleep stages is essential for assessing sleep quality and diagnosing sleep disorders. However, manual inspection of EEG characteristics for each stage is time-consuming and prone to human error. Although machine learning and deep learning methods have been actively developed, they continue to face challenges arising from the non-stationarity and variability of electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals across diverse clinical configurations, often resulting in poor generalization. In this work, we propose SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework for heterogeneous EEG-EOG representation learning. SleepDIFFormer is trained across multiple sleep staging datasets, each treated as a source domain, with the goal of generalizing to unseen target domains. Specifically, it employs a Multi-channel Differential Transformer Architecture (MDTA) designed to process raw EEG and EOG signals while incorporating cross-domain alignment. Our approach mitigates spatial and temporal attention noise and learns a domain-invariant EEG-EOG representation through feature distribution alignment across datasets, thereby enhancing generalization to new domains. Empirically, we evaluated SleepDIFFormer on five diverse sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings and benchmarked it against existing approaches, achieving superior performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation analyses and interpretation of the differential attention weights demonstrated their relevance to learning discriminative sleep EEG representations. These findings support the development of more generalizable approaches to automated sleep-stage classification. Our source code and checkpoint are made publicly available at https://github.com/Ben1001409/SleepDIFFormer.

papers.title: REM Atonia Index Cutoffs for REM Sleep Without Atonia: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis of Adult Diagnostic Performance.
papers.abstract: To synthesize evidence on REM Atonia Index (RAI) thresholds and reference values, quantify adult diagnostic performance for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and distinguish diagnostic cutoffs from physiological reference limits and pediatric values. Methods: We conducted a focused systematic review of studies using automated RAI, rescreening studies from a previous review and updating PubMed/MEDLINE through July 27, 2026. Adult diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with a bivariate binomial-normal random-effects model. Continuous RAI differences were pooled as raw mean differences. Normative adult and pediatric evidence was synthesized separately because these represented different estimands. The review was retrospectively registered in OSF Registries on August 20, 2026 (https://osf.io/v3kqa). Thirty unique studies were included. Eight adult studies contributed to the diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis; thresholds ranged from 0.80 to 0.90. Pooled sensitivity was 0.850 (95% CI, 0.766-0.908) and specificity 0.895 (95% CI, 0.814-0.944). Eight studies contributed continuous data; RAI was lower in RBD by a pooled mean difference of -0.263 (95% CI, -0.335 to -0.190). Only two methodologically non-equivalent adult studies provided physiological reference limits, 0.85 and 0.91, precluding pooling. Pediatric evidence supported age-conditioned interpretation. Adult chin-EMG RAI shows good overall discrimination of established RBD, but current evidence does not support a universal numerical boundary for REM sleep without atonia. Evidence defining physiological reference limits is substantially less developed than diagnostic evidence, and normal RAI varies with age. RAI should therefore be reported continuously, with thresholds interpreted according to their intended diagnostic or physiological purpose.

papers.title: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: Unloading the Respiratory System with Expiratory Pressure.
papers.abstract: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is traditionally interpreted through the lens of coexistent obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the mechanisms by which continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) improves daytime hypercapnia without providing ventilatory support remain incompletely explained. This Perspective proposes that abdominal obesity-induced depletion of expiratory reserve volume (ERV) and functional residual capacity (FRC), with consequent reduction in end-expiratory lung volume (EELV), may represent upstream mechanical abnormalities linking OSA, increased work of breathing, sleep hypoventilation, and daytime hypercapnia. Reduced EELV worsens pharyngeal collapsibility by decreasing caudal traction, while simultaneously shifting tidal volume toward a mechanically inefficient portion of the respiratory system curve, characterized by impaired compliance, and increased elastic, resistive respiratory work and possibly threshold loading. Within this framework, OHS emerges when respiratory burden (the mechanical load on the pulmonary apparatus due to excess weight) exceeds ventilatory reserve (an ensemble of respiratory drive and its modifiers such as sleep-state control, leptin signaling, and genetic factors). CPAP and expiratory PAP may provide, in addition to upper-airway splinting, a mechanical unloading by raising EELV, improving respiratory mechanics, and reducing the pressure cost of ventilation. In this context, weight loss represents the ultimate structural unloading therapy, whereas pressure support may be required when unloading alone is insufficient to restore adequate ventilation. Future studies should measure ERV, FRC/EELV, respiratory effort, and mechanics to better phenotype OHS, and understand whether optimizing expiratory pressure before adding ventilatory support actually improves ventilation.

papers.title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study.
papers.abstract: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.

papers.title: Three-month follow-up after discontinuation of steam-assisted respiratory muscle training in mild-to-moderate obstructive sleep apnea: an exploratory polysomnographic study.
papers.abstract: To explore polysomnographic findings three months after discontinuation of steam-assisted respiratory muscle training (RMT) in mild-to-moderate obstructive sleep apnea. This exploratory secondary follow-up included 33 of 48 intervention entrants who completed polysomnography at baseline, after 12 weeks of training, and three months after cessation. The primary analysis used repeated-measures ANOVA (RM-ANOVA). Distributional diagnostics and exact Friedman sensitivity analyses were conducted for eight sleep-stage and periodic limb movement outcomes. Conventional respiratory-event indices showed no overall time effect (all p ≥ 0.3). Flow limitation differed across visits (p = 0.02), without an immediate post-intervention reduction. The RM-ANOVA identified visit differences in REM latency (169.9 ± 74.9 min at baseline, 138.8 ± 66.4 min post-intervention, and 134.0 ± 66.5 min at follow-up; p = 0.003), N1 proportion (6.6 ± 4.0%, 10.8 ± 5.9%, and 11.2 ± 6.1%, respectively; p = 0.002), and PLMS-related arousal index (1.3 ± 2.1/h, 0.6 ± 1.1/h, and 0.7 ± 1.4/h, respectively; p = 0.01) and count (9.3 ± 15.2, 4.3 ± 7.9, and 5.2 ± 10.0, respectively; p = 0.02). Exact Friedman analyses yielded visit differences for N1 (p = 0.002) and the PLMS-related arousal index and count (p = 0.01 and 0.02), but not REM latency (p = 0.1). This exploratory follow-up identified differences in N1 proportion and PLMS-related arousal measures across visits, supported by sensitivity analyses, while no overall visit differences were detected in conventional respiratory-event indices. REM latency differed significantly across visits in RM-ANOVA, but not in the sensitivity analysis. These observations warrant further investigation in controlled studies; the single-arm design and absence of an adaptation night prevent attribution to steam-assisted RMT or confirmation of lasting clinical benefit. GOV: NCT05320952.

papers.title: Single-Lead EEG-based virtual reality motion sickness detection using interpretable feature selection.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a key method for detecting virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), but multi-lead recordings and high-dimensional features increase processing complexity, device cost, and user burden. This study proposes a SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based single-lead modeling and feature-screening framework to reduce the number of EEG leads and feature dimensions for lightweight VRMS detection. Six classical deep-learning EEG decoding models were used to assess the contribution of each lead via SHAP values and identify the optimal single lead. Handcrafted features were then extracted and selected using a correlation-SHAP strategy, and XGBoost was adopted for final classification. FT11 showed competitive and relatively consistent performance across the evaluated models and was selected as the target lead after integrating SHAP-based lead importance, single-lead classification performance, frequency-band differences, and physiological relevance. Under the window-level tenfold cross-validation protocol used in this study, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 87.53% ± 0.73% using seven selected features, which was 9.55 percentage points lower than the full-lead full-feature model and 0.69 percentage points lower than the single-lead full-feature model. These findings demonstrate an interpretable framework for identifying a compact single-lead and feature configuration for VRMS-related EEG discrimination. An additional post hoc LOSO test of the globally selected configuration showed limited performance on held-out participants. Because the lead, classifier, and feature configuration had been selected globally before LOSO testing, these results should not be interpreted as a fully independent estimate of cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: Considering counterfactual prediction models in sleep research: A demonstration of incident stroke prediction in an observational cohort study.
papers.abstract: Data-driven risk prediction algorithms are increasingly common. However, studies suggesting that a single set of variables are most "important" within a given risk prediction model ignore the reality that other equally useful models containing entirely different features may exist. We aim to use a novel approach (Model Path Selection) to demonstrate that, for any given health outcome, there are likely many comparable counterfactual models including different sets of variables. We focus on incident stroke as a scientifically meaningful outcome to motivate this demonstration. Model Path Selection uses an iterative model-building procedure to illustrate a set of counterfactual prediction models ("paths"). We applied Model Path Selection to Sleep Heart Health Study data (N = 4,512 adults) to predict 5-year incident stroke, considering 30 features comprising demographics, self-reported and measured medical risk factors, polysomnography, and self-reported sleep. Area Under the Curve was estimated for each resulting path based on 10-fold cross-validation. Model Path Selection identified 61 unique counterfactual models. 13 of these achieved Area Under the Curves between 0.81 and 0.82. Area Under the Curves of the remaining models ranged from 0.53 to 0.68 (median 0.61). All 13 top models included age plus various combinations of other features (polysomnography indices, body mass index, and/or the Short Form 36 mental and physical component scores). Model Path Selection can illuminate counterfactual prediction models, differentiate features that may be uniquely predictive from those that can be swapped out with other features, enhance reproducibility, inform the design of clinically practical predictive tools, and suggest sleep-related risk factors to be targeted for health promotion.

papers.title: Comparing re-referencing methods for human intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) involves the implantation of depth electrodes in the brain to monitor epileptic seizures for surgical feasibility. As the electrodes advance into deeper limbic structures, the macro contacts distributed along the shaft record electrical activity from more lateral sites, while a bundled array of microwires simultaneously captures highly localised signals from the tip of the electrode. In a clinical setting these electrical signals are recorded relative to a reference signal, which may be sub-optimal for subsequent analyses that are unrelated to clinical objectives. Therefore, a secondary re-referencing operation is often undertaken to transform the signal in relation to a specific hypothesis. Despite a recent surge in SEEG studies, comparative studies on the much-understudied issue of re-referencing are sparse. Here, we analyse data collected from 16 human patients during an episodic memory task and comparatively apply a range of re-referencing methods to both macro contact and micro-wire data. We find that the choice of method changes the proportion of trials that survive artefact rejection, low frequency power, and the aperiodic background against which that power is read. In the hippocampal recordings, however, no method differed from any other in the size of a memory effect in power or spike-field coherence. This early transformative decision therefore bears on how the signal is described. We found no evidence that it changes the detectability of the behavioural effects tested here, and no method reversed the direction of a memory effect.

papers.title: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalogram (aEEG): A bedside window into newborn brain function in the NICU.
papers.abstract: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG) remains an important tool for bedside neonatal brain monitoring. The rapid application of aEEG offers critical practical advantages for bedside clinicians assessing infants at risk for brain injury. aEEG has a distinct clinical niche in evaluations for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and as a first-line tool for seizure detection, alongside conventional video electroencephalogram (cEEG). Ultimately, the integration of aEEG with a broader multimodal neuromonitoring framework enhances neurodevelopmental prognostication and facilitates individualized bedside interventions, solidifying its relevance in contemporary neonatal neurocritical care.

papers.title: Composite sleep patterns and the allergy-related composite outcome among American and Chinese older adults: exploration of depressive symptoms as a potential mediator.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms commonly co-occur in older adults, but their associations with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes and the role of depressive symptoms remain unclear. We analyzed 1,562 participants aged ≥60 years from NHANES 2005-2006. A composite sleep pattern combined sleep duration, trouble sleeping, and diagnosed sleep disorders. The allergy-related composite outcome comprised elevated total immunoglobulin E and seven questionnaire-assessed disease or symptom outcomes. Survey-weighted logistic regression evaluated associations. Depressive symptoms were assessed with a modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8), and statistical mediation examined indirect associations through its continuous score. We also conducted a complementary longitudinal analysis in 6,146 Chinese older adults from CHARLS. Poor versus healthy sleep was associated with higher odds of the allergy-related composite outcome (OR 2.100; 95% CI 1.328-3.322), wheeze (OR 2.148; 95% CI 1.296-3.559), and sneeze (OR 1.636; 95% CI 1.135-2.357). The estimated indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 22.5% of the total association. In CHARLS, impaired sleep quality was associated with incident asthma (OR 1.689; 95% CI 1.254-2.275), and the corresponding indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 28.3% of the total association. Poor sleep was associated with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes among US older adults, while CHARLS provided complementary longitudinal evidence for incident asthma. Depressive symptoms statistically accounted for part of the observed sleep-allergy association.

papers.title: Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
papers.abstract: Pharmacotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet some individuals show partial or inadequate response associated with adverse effects. These limitations have prompted interest in adjunctive or alternative interventions. Electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback is a non-pharmacological intervention for ADHD, which enables self-regulation of neural activity. This systematic review synthesised clinical, cognitive, and electrophysiological outcomes of EEG neurofeedback in adult ADHD, and examined standard versus personalised training protocols. Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, Ovid, Web of Science) were searched from 1960 to October 2025 for this PROSPERO-registered review (ID: CRD420251020898). Eligible studies included adults (≥ 18 years) with a formal ADHD diagnosis undergoing EEG neurofeedback. Outcomes comprised symptom severity, cognitive performance, electrophysiology, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I V2. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) met inclusion criteria. Protocols included theta/beta (n = 1), slow cortical potential (n = 1), alpha downregulation training (n = 1) and personalised approaches guided by individual alpha peak frequency (n = 3) or QEEG profiles (n = 1). Naturalistic and personalised studies reported large symptom reductions, whereas RCTs revealed small, generally non-significant effects relative to controls. Cognitive improvements were inconsistently reported and largely attributable to practice effects. Electrophysiological changes were protocol-specific without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were observed. Evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, small samples, variable controls, inconsistent learning metrics, and risk of bias. Current RCTs do not demonstrate evidence of efficacy over placebo. Blinded, adequately powered trials using standardised learning measures are needed to clarify mechanisms of neurofeedback.

papers.title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
papers.abstract: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited. This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored. Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects. Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea is frequent in patients with Long COVID fatigue but is not significantly associated with alterations of quality of life and cognition.
papers.abstract: Neurologic manifestations of Long COVID, also called post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), include fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbances, and headaches, which can be debilitating. Since these symptoms overlap with those of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), we sought to determine the prevalence of OSA in the population of a Neuro-COVID-19 clinic. We performed home sleep testing in 100 consecutive patients with Long COVID and no prior history of OSA who reported fatigue after an episode of COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. The average age was 46.4 years and 70% of patients were female. OSA was present in 53% of patients, including 33% with mild OSA (apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) 5-14.9) and 20% with moderate to severe OSA (AHI ≥ 15). Male sex, higher age, and body mass index were significantly associated with OSA. However, there were no significant differences in other comorbidities, Long COVID symptom burden, quality of life measures (QoL), and objective cognitive function test results between groups. Additionally, multiple linear regression models demonstrated that neither AHI nor mean desaturation nadir were significant predictors of QoL or cognitive function. Although OSA is nearly twice as prevalent among our study participants compared to the general adult population of the US, it was not significantly associated with Long COVID symptoms, alteration of QoL, or objective cognitive dysfunction. However, 20% of patients were diagnosed with moderate to severe OSA, a clinically significant finding that warrants intervention to prevent irreversible cardiopulmonary complications.

papers.title: Longitudinal sleep duration trajectories and their association with cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity risk in postmenopausal women: evidence from the CHARLS study.
papers.abstract: To investigate the association between longitudinal sleep duration trajectories and the risk of cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity (CRMM) in a population of postmenopausal women. A total of 2,859 postmenopausal women from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) were included, with 4 repeated measurements of night sleep duration collected from 2011 to 2018. Group-based trajectory modeling was adopted to identify distinct sleep duration trajectory patterns. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations between sleep trajectories and incident CRMM ascertained between 2018 and 2020. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were further conducted to validate the robustness of the findings. Three sleep duration trajectory patterns were identified: normal-stable (33.9% of the cohort), normal-fluctuating decline (52.0%), and short-rapid decline (14.1%). During a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome (incident CRMM) occurred in 108 participants (3.8%). Compared with normal-stable group, those in normal-fluctuating decline and short-rapid decline groups had an increased risk of CRMM (ORs of 2.30 [95%CI, 1.35-3.91] and 3.75 [95%CI, 1.99-7.07], respectively) after adjustment for multiple covariates. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these associations, which were independent of key baseline characteristics and missing data. In postmenopausal women, short and declining sleep duration trajectories are strong, independent risk factors for CRMM. Public health and clinical interventions should prioritize maintaining stable, adequate sleep to mitigate multimorbidity risk in this population.

papers.title: Comparative effects of exercise modalities on sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders: A systematic review with pairwise, network, and dose-responsemeta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Exercise may improve sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders, but the comparative effects of different exercise modalities and the dose-response relationship remain unclear. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to May 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials examining the effects of exercise interventions on sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders. Two independent reviewers assessed study quality, and random-effects pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses were performed to evaluate the effects of different exercise interventions and doses on sleep quality. The analysis included 23 randomized controlled trials involving 1,478 middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders. Pairwise meta-analysis showed that exercise reduced Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores but had no significant effect on Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) scores. Bayesian network meta-analysis showed that, compared with the control group, aerobic exercise (SMD = 1.34, 95% CrI: 0.86∼1.82), mind-body exercise (SMD = 0.64, 95% CrI: 0.30∼0.97), and combined exercise (SMD = 0.60, 95% CrI: 0.13∼1.07) may improve PSQI scores. The dose-response analysis suggested an inverted U-shaped association, with the largest predicted effect occurring near 539 MET-min/week within the observed dose range. Low-to moderate-certainty evidence suggests that aerobic, mind-body, and combined exercise may reduce PSQI scores, with a nonlinear dose-response relationship.

papers.title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction.
papers.abstract: Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

papers.title: The qualitative exploration of work productivity among chronic rhinitis patients.

It contributes to socioeconomic costs through decreased productivity, including absenteeism and presenteeism. Data saturation was reached, and thematic analysis was performed using Atlas.ti. Eight themes were identified: absence during working hours, work limitations, disruption of social interactions, reduced work efficiency, emotional disturbances, weaknesses in compliance with work procedures, sleepiness at work, and negative perceptions from colleagues. Chronic rhinitis significantly affects work productivity, leading to absenteeism, reduced efficiency, and workplace stigma. These findings highlight the need for targeted management strategies to improve work performance and reduce the negative impact of chronic rhinitis on affected individuals.

papers.title: Sleep duration and risk of microvascular complications in type 2 diabetes: A prospective cohort study.

papers.title: Is Less More? Exploring the Visual Processes of Minimalist and Complex Photography Through Eye Tracking and EEG.
papers.abstract: In a world filled with an overwhelming amount of visual information, the clean and distinctive visual style of minimalist photography stands out. However, empirical research on how minimalist style affects visual cognition and psychological responses remains limited. The present study investigated the effects of photographic style (minimalist versus complex) on viewers' visual behavior, emotional responses, and brainwave state by conducting quantitative psychological experiments. Thirty participants viewed photographs in one of the two styles. Eye-tracking, consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG), and subjective psychological assessment data were collected, enabling comprehensive evaluation of how the participants looked at, responded to, and emotionally engaged with the images. At the level of visual behavior, minimalism elicited significantly reduced number of fixations and saccades, but the duration of a single fixation is significantly longer, and the heatmap hotspots are highly concentrated, presenting a focused processing pattern of fewer but longer gazes. On a psychological level, minimalism evoked significantly less feeling of complexity and greater relaxation, although there was no significant difference in the aesthetics score between the two styles. In terms of brainwave state, viewing minimalist images resulted in significantly higher attention eSense levels, while the meditation eSense level did not show a significant difference. The results of this study therefore show that minimalist composition may influence the visual search pattern to be more focused, which is compatible with the tendency of simplified organization predicted by the principle of simplification. This study not only deepens the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms of minimalist aesthetics, but also provides practical reference for visual communication and image creation of minimalist composition serving as an effective strategy for guiding the eyes toward the core subject.

papers.title: Mapping mental health complexity in esports: an exploratory psychosocial network approach.
papers.abstract: The rapid rise in popularity of esports has brought increased attention to the unique mental health challenges faced by esports players, yet research in this area remains in its infancy. Early research suggests a substantial mental health burden and has examined associations between esports-specific stressors, mental health, and sleep disturbances. However, much of this work has relied on traditional methodologies, providing limited insight into how affective, psychosocial, sleep-related, and esports-specific indicators are organised within this competitive performance environment. To address this gap, we developed a bespoke 17-item questionnaire tailored for Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) network analysis, an exploratory approach for mapping the conditional dependency structure of complex multivariate systems such as mental health. A total of 1025 esports players from over 60 countries completed the survey. Game-related thought preoccupation, a core feature of gaming disorder, emerged as the most robust structural sink node, downstream of several psychosocial indicators, raising the hypothesis that it represents a compound indicator of broader upstream psychosocial strain. Depressed mood occupied an upstream position within the network, an observation that held more robustly for the psychopathological subnetwork as a whole than for depressed mood as the single source. Mental fatigue occupied an intermediate, connecting position between affective variables and the sleep and fatigue indicators. Its high prevalence, together with a positioning upstream of the sleep indicators, suggests that it may warrant closer examination in future research on training load, recovery, and sleep in esports, though this ordering rested on edges with moderate directional support. Emotion control and a sense of autonomy appeared to connect upstream affective distress with downstream esports-specific indicators such as esports-related stress, though was the least stable of the structural features identified. Collectively, these findings provide an exploratory map of how mental health-relevant indicators were organised in this performance environment, and generate concrete, testable hypotheses for future longitudinal, experimental, and intervention research.

These results demonstrate the utility of gut microbiota, particularly SCFA-producing taxa, in the early identification of prodromal PD. Integration with select clinical features further improves model performance, supporting their potential role in early diagnostic frameworks.

papers.title: Effects of an Esketamine-Containing Induction Regimen on Postoperative Sleep, Analgesia, and Postpartum Depression in Parturients with Sleep Disorders Undergoing Cesarean Section Under General Anesthesia: A Double-Blind Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Preoperative sleep disturbances in parturients undergoing cesarean section correlate with exacerbated postoperative pain and an elevated risk of postpartum depression. Although esketamine demonstrates analgesic and antidepressant benefits in the general cesarean population, its combined effects on sleep, analgesia, and mood remain poorly characterized in patients with pre-existing sleep impairment. This study investigated the efficacy of an esketamine‑containing induction regimen on postoperative sleep quality, analgesia, and early depressive symptoms in parturients with PSQI‑defined preoperative sleep disorders scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 90 parturients scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either an esketamine-containing induction regimen (esketamine 0.25 mg/kg plus propofol 1.0 mg/kg; n=45) or a standard induction regimen (saline plus propofol 2.0 mg/kg; n=45). All 90 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (missing data imputed), and 84 (41 vs 43) were included in the complete-case sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1, assessed using an 11-point sleep Numerical Rating Scale (NRS; 0=best, 10=worst; 24-hour recall). Secondary outcomes included sleep NRS scores on POD 3 and POD 42, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) on POD 42 (exploratory); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores at 2, 12, 24, and 48 hours, and rescue analgesic consumption over 72 hours; and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores on POD 3 and POD 42 (≥13 indicating a positive result). The esketamine regimen significantly improved the primary outcome (sleep NRS on POD 1; mean difference [MD] = 3.0, 95% CI: 2.0 to 4.0; P < 0.001). Exploratory secondary outcomes showed early pain benefits and reduced rescue analgesia (risk ratio [RR] = 3.33, 95% CI: 0.98 to 11.32; absolute risk difference = 15.5%, 95% CI: 0.7% to 30.21%), but these differences were small with wide intervals. Continuous EPDS scores were lower on POD 3 (P = 0.004), while the exploratory binary analysis (EPDS ≥ 13) was not significant (RR = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.56 to 2.66; P = 0.613). No serious adverse events occurred; however, the trial was not powered for safety outcomes. An esketamine-containing induction regimen was associated with improved early sleep quality on POD 1 in parturients with preoperative sleep disorders undergoing cesarean delivery under general anesthesia. However, because the trial was not powered for secondary outcomes or safety, and the differing propofol doses prevent isolation of esketamine's specific effect, these secondary findings are exploratory. Further adequately powered trials are required to confirm these results and evaluate safety. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300078490.

papers.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique. In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11.84 percentage points [95% CI, -22.98 to -0.69]; relative risk [RR], 0.52 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.047). The per-protocol (PP) sensitivity analysis yielded similar results (12.8% vs 24.2%; RR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.043). PSD on POD 1 did not differ between the groups. No between-group differences in postoperative anxiety or depression scores were noted. Postoperative pain scores at 30 minutes were significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.001). Dreaming was more frequent in the esketamine group (21.4% vs 11.2%; P = 0.048), and the time to full alertness (12 [10-14] vs 11 [9-13] minutes; P = 0.002) and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay (34 [30-37] vs 31 [29-34] minutes; P = 0.005) were modestly longer. A single subanesthetic dose of esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of short-term PSD on POD 3 in women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings. China Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500105998.

papers.title: A general condition for fast rates in multi-group learning
papers.abstract: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must control its excess risk simultaneously over overlapping groups. Tosh and Hsu (2022) obtained $1/\sqrt{n}$ slow rates via a reduction to online learning with sleeping experts, and $1/n$ rates only under realizability (and for a different strategy). We identify a group-wise Bernstein condition under which the same adaptive predictor attains the fast rate $1/n$ without knowing whether the condition holds, while retaining the slow rates on the groups where it fails. The condition is implied by some natural assumptions weaker than realizability. Lower bounds show that weakened versions leave every learner with slow rates. Intermediate rates under relaxed conditions and an extension to VC classes are also obtained.

papers.title: An incidental heterozygous ATP7B nonsense variant leading to a diagnostic pitfall for Wilson disease: a pediatric case report.
papers.abstract: Wilson disease (WD) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7B, resulting in impaired copper transport and progressive copper accumulation, most prominently affecting the liver. With the growing use of genetic testing, incidental detection of ATP7B pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in individuals without typical hepatic phenotypes can prompt overdiagnosis and unnecessary investigations. This case highlights the importance of interpreting a single heterozygous ATP7B variant in the context of phenotype and a standardized biochemical diagnostic pathway for WD. A 13-year-old Han Chinese boy presented with recurrent brief paroxysmal attacks for > 1 year, markedly worsened over the preceding month. Episodes were triggered by rising from sitting, characterized by transient postural instability with unilateral head deviation and ipsilateral dystonic/choreiform movements, lasted ~ 10 s, and resolved spontaneously. Consciousness was preserved, with no incontinence, convulsions, or postictal symptoms. Interictal neurological examination was normal. Ambulatory EEG monitoring captured three typical attacks without epileptiform discharges or ictal EEG correlates, and brain MRI was unremarkable. A slit-lamp examination revealed no Kayser-Fleischer ring. A low serum copper level (9.43 µmol/L; reference 10.50-29.90) prompted further evaluation; genetic testing incidentally identified a heterozygous ATP7B variant (NM_000053.4:c.2851 C > T; p.Gln951Ter), reported as likely pathogenic. WD was considered. However, ceruloplasmin was normal (231.6 mg/L; reference 200.0-420.0 mg/L), ceruloplasmin oxidase activity measured by the p-phenylenediamine method was normal (0.372 OD; reference > 0.200 OD), liver biochemistry was normal (ALT 11 U/L, AST 16 U/L, GGT 14 U/L; bilirubin within reference range), and abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver and biliary tree. Crucially, a follow-up quantitative 24-hour urinary copper test was strictly normal, and parental segregation analysis confirmed that the ATP7B variant represented a paternally inherited heterozygous state without biochemical evidence of Wilson disease, making active Wilson disease highly unlikely. This case illustrates a critical diagnostic pitfall: incidental heterozygous ATP7B variants can trigger severe diagnostic anchoring bias. To prevent overdiagnosis, genetic findings must be subordinated to strict phenotype-driven evaluations, formal Leipzig scoring, and definitive biochemical gold standards.

papers.title: MRI Characterization of Structural Brain Abnormalities in NGLY1 Deficiency.
papers.abstract: NGLY1 (N-Glycanase 1) deficiency is an ultrarare autosomal recessive disorder affecting ~165 patients worldwide, characterized by developmental delay, hyperkinetic movement disorders and shortened life expectancy. Despite its severe neurological manifestations, comprehensive neuroimaging characterization has been limited to case reports and small descriptive studies. Our objective was to investigate alterations in brain morphology in patients with NGLY1 deficiency and determine whether these metrics associate with clinical phenotypes. This case series analysed real-world MRI scans performed on 11 patients with molecularly diagnosed NGLY1 deficiency between 1999 and 2023 at sites across the globe. Ages ranged from 2 to 19 years at scan time (five female and six male). Cortical and subcortical morphology, including subcortical volume and cortical thickness, surface area, volume and curvature, was measured with three-dimensional T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. Z scores were calculated using normative models from CentileBrain for patients > 3 years old or custom models for patients < 3 years old. Clinical phenotypes were matched to Human Phenotype Ontology codes. Sixteen scans from 11 patients met quality criteria for analysis. Both age groups (under and over 3 years old) showed significantly reduced subcortical volumes, particularly in bilateral thalamus and putamen. Younger patients demonstrated widespread reductions in cortical surface area, volume and curvature, indicating altered gyrification patterns. Older patients showed thinner dorsal and thicker ventral cortical regions with limited surface area reductions. Thalamic volume reduction in older patients correlated with gait disturbance, dysphagia and EEG abnormalities, with additional cortical associations with sleep and hearing abnormalities. Seizure presence in younger patients correlated with altered cortical thickness, surface area and curvature patterns. NGLY1 deficiency is associated with pervasive alterations in brain development affecting both subcortical and cortical morphology. Age-dependent patterns of cortical alterations indicate disrupted neurodevelopmental trajectories that may reflect impaired neuronal migration and/or altered synaptic pruning. Correlations with clinical variables suggest that these measures may serve as useful biomarkers for tracking disease progression and/or treatment efficacy. These findings provide a comprehensive neuroimaging characterization of NGLY1 Deficiency and establish a foundation for understanding brain structure-function relationships in this ultrarare disorder.

papers.title: Early Postoperative Psychological Resilience Patterns and Associated Factors in Patients with Knee Stiffness Undergoing Arthroscopic Release Surgery: A Latent Class Growth Model Study.
papers.abstract: Knee stiffness substantially impairs mobility and quality of life. Although arthroscopic release can improve joint function, little is known about early postoperative changes in psychological resilience among these patients. This study aimed to identify heterogeneous early postoperative psychological resilience patterns in patients with knee stiffness undergoing arthroscopic release surgery and to explore factors associated with pattern membership. A prospective observational study was conducted among patients undergoing arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. Psychological resilience was assessed using the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale at four time points: admission before surgery, 3 days after surgery, 2 weeks after surgery, and 1 month after surgery. Latent class growth modeling was used to identify early postoperative resilience pattern groups. Univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression were conducted to explore factors associated with pattern membership. Multicollinearity among candidate predictors was assessed before multivariable modeling. A total of 240 patients completed all four assessments. The LCGM identified three early postoperative psychological resilience pattern groups: the Low Resilience Declining Group (17.1%), the Moderate Resilience Stable Group (68.8%), and the High Resilience Increasing Group (14.2%). Multinomial logistic regression using standardized continuous psychosocial predictors showed that, compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Low Resilience Declining Group had lower perceived social support and poorer sleep quality. Compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Moderate Resilience Stable Group were more likely to have a primary-school education or below, lower perceived social support, and lower ERRI scores. Psychological resilience showed heterogeneous patterns during the early postoperative period after arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. The findings may help identify patients who are psychologically vulnerable during early recovery, but should be interpreted as exploratory because of the single-center design, short follow-up duration, and limited subgroup sizes. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up and orthopedic outcome measures are needed to validate these early postoperative patterns and clarify their clinical significance. papers.title: Comparative analysis of pain experience and quality of life in patients with oral lichen planus and burning mouth syndrome.
papers.abstract: Oral lichen planus (OLP) and burning mouth syndrome (BMS) are chronic oral conditions associated with persistent pain, but direct comparisons of their pain profiles and contributing factors remain limited. This study compared factors influencing pain perception between OLP and BMS. This cross-sectional study included 46 patients with OLP and 50 with BMS. Pain characteristics, pain catastrophizing, and quality of life were assessed using the Brief Pain Inventory-Korean version, Pain Catastrophizing Scale-Korean version, and a Korean-language Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders Quality of Life questionnaire. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; Mann-Whitney U or independent t-tests were applied accordingly, and effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d. Pain intensity predictors were identified using stepwise multiple linear regression. Patients with BMS reported higher pain intensity (p ≤ 0.003, d = -1.22 to -0.63) and catastrophizing (p = 0.005, d = -0.56) than those with OLP, whereas patients with OLP showed greater mastication-related pain interference (p = 0.002, d = 0.74) and poorer quality of life (p = 0.020, d = 0.50). Regression identified mastication and rumination in OLP (adjusted R2 = 0.419) and sleep disturbance, rumination, and magnification in BMS (adjusted R2 = 0.454) as primary predictors. Age stratification revealed an opposite age-pain relationship: older patients with BMS (>60 years) had higher pain intensity (p < 0.001), whereas younger patients with OLP (≤60 years) reported higher pain intensity (p = 0.037). Pain interference was more interconnected across life domains in OLP (27 correlations with |r| > 0.5) than in BMS (6 correlations). OLP and BMS exhibit distinct pain profiles, with OLP characterized by widespread functional interference influenced by mastication-related and cognitive factors, and BMS marked by higher pain intensity with prominent psychological contributors. Condition-specific strategies incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy targeting rumination may improve pain-related outcomes.
